title: Shortest Path in a Grid with Obstacles Elimination
prompt: You are given an `m x n` binary matrix `grid` where `0` represents an empty cell and `1` represents an obstacle. You can move 4-directionally between empty cells. You are also given an integer `k` representing the maximum number of obstacles you can eliminate (walk through) during the path. Return the minimum number of steps to walk from the top-left corner `(0, 0)` to the bottom-right corner `(m-1, n-1)`, given that you can eliminate at most `k` obstacles. If it is not possible, return `-1`.

examples.explanation: Eliminating one obstacle lets you cut through a wall and reach the destination in 6 steps; without elimination the path would be longer or impossible.
Even eliminating one obstacle isn't enough to break through and reach the bottom-right corner.

hints: This is BFS on an expanded state space: a state isn't just a cell, it's (row, col, obstacles eliminated so far), since the same cell might be worth revisiting if you arrive with more elimination budget remaining.
From state (r, c, remaining), moving into a neighbor that's an obstacle costs one unit of `remaining`; moving into an empty cell costs none. Only enqueue a state if remaining stays >= 0.

Track visited as (r, c, remaining) triples — or optimize by tracking the best (maximum) remaining budget seen so far at each cell, and skip a state if you've already visited that cell with an equal or better remaining budget, since arriving with less budget can never be better.

solution.approach: Treat each BFS state as (row, col, obstacles eliminated so far) rather than just a cell, since reaching the same cell with a different elimination budget can lead to different future possibilities. Run BFS layer by layer (each layer is one step); when moving into an obstacle cell, increment the elimination count only if it doesn't exceed k. To keep the state space bounded, skip revisiting a cell if it's already been reached with an equal-or-fewer eliminations used (a strictly worse or equal state can't do better later). Because k can be at least m+n-2 (the minimum possible path length) - 1, if k >= m+n-2 the direct Manhattan-distance path always works as a shortcut.
